title: POSSIBILITY & DEDUCTION
notes:
✓ Possibility → expresses that something may or may not be true or may happen.

✓ Deduction → a conclusion reached by using available evidence or logical reasoning.

✓ English commonly uses modal verbs to express different degrees of certainty.

✓ She may be at home. → possible.
✓ She must be at home. → strong logical conclusion.
✓ She can't be at home. → strong logical conclusion that something is impossible.

◆ Basic scale →
✓ Certain → must
✓ Very likely → should / ought to
✓ Possible → may / might / could
✓ Impossible → can't / couldn't

⚠ These meanings depend on context and whether the deduction concerns the present, past, or future.

title: MODAL VERBS FOR POSSIBILITY
notes:
✓ MAY → something is possible.
✓ MIGHT → possibility, often weaker or more tentative than may.
✓ COULD → possible situation or one possible explanation.
✓ CAN → general possibility, especially things that can happen generally.
✓ MAY NOT → possible negative situation.
✓ MIGHT NOT → possible negative situation, often more tentative.

✓ She may come tonight.
✓ She might come tonight.
✓ She could come tonight.

✓ In many everyday contexts, may/might/could overlap in meaning, but their degree of certainty and context can differ.

title: MAY
notes:
✓ May + V1 → possibility in the present or future.

✓ It may rain this evening.
✓ She may be at home.

✓ May not → something is possibly not true or may possibly not happen.
✓ He may not come tonight.

⚠ May is also used for formal permission, but in possibility/deduction questions it expresses uncertainty.

✓ May I leave early? → permission.
✓ He may leave early. → possibility.

✓ May generally sounds more formal than might in many contexts.

title: MIGHT
notes:
✓ Might + V1 → expresses possibility or uncertainty.

✓ It might rain later.
✓ She might be busy.

✓ Might often presents a possibility more tentatively than a strong prediction.
✓ We might go to the beach tomorrow.

✓ Might not → something is possibly not true or may not happen.
✓ He might not come.

✓ Might is especially useful when the speaker does not want to express strong certainty.

title: COULD FOR POSSIBILITY
notes:
✓ Could + V1 → expresses a possible future or present situation.

✓ It could rain tonight.
✓ She could be at the library.

✓ Could can present one possible explanation among several.
✓ The lights are off. They could be asleep.

✓ Could also express ability in other contexts.
✓ She could swim when she was five. → past ability.
✓ She could be swimming now. → possibility.

✓ Always use context to determine whether could means ability or possibility.

title: CAN FOR GENERAL POSSIBILITY
notes:
✓ Can + V1 → often expresses general or theoretical possibility.

✓ Accidents can happen.
✓ Winters can be very cold here.

⚠ Can is generally not the normal choice for a specific uncertain event.

❌ It can rain tomorrow. → unnatural if you simply mean 'perhaps'.
✓ It may/might/could rain tomorrow.

✓ General possibility → can.
✓ Specific uncertain possibility → may/might/could.

title: MUST FOR DEDUCTION
notes:
✓ Must + V1/be → strong logical deduction based on evidence.

✓ The lights are on. They must be home.
✓ She has studied all night. She must be tired.

✓ Meaning → the speaker believes the conclusion is almost certainly true based on evidence.

⚠ This is different from obligation.

✓ You must wear a seat belt. → obligation.
✓ You must be tired after that journey. → deduction.

✓ Deduction meaning → 'I strongly conclude that this is true.'

title: CAN'T / CANNOT FOR DEDUCTION
notes:
✓ Can't + V1/be → strong logical conclusion that something is impossible or almost certainly not true.

✓ He can't be at home; I just saw him at school.
✓ That can't be John's car. His car is blue.

✓ Meaning → the available evidence makes the situation impossible or extremely unlikely.

⚠ Can't for deduction is not simply the same as 'must not.'

✓ He can't be serious. → I conclude that it is impossible/unbelievable that he is serious.
✓ You mustn't enter. → prohibition.

❌ He mustn't be at home. → normally interpreted as prohibition/strong negative obligation, not the standard deduction form.
✓ He can't be at home.

title: MUST BE VS MAY/MIGHT/COULD BE
notes:
◆ Degree of certainty:

✓ MUST BE → very strong deduction.
✓ The ground is wet. It must be raining.

✓ MAY BE → possible.
✓ She may be at work.

✓ MIGHT BE → possible but tentative.
✓ She might be at work.

✓ COULD BE → one possible explanation.
✓ She could be at work.

✓ CAN'T BE → strong negative deduction.
✓ She can't be at work; the office is closed.

✓ Remember → must = strong positive conclusion; can't = strong negative conclusion; may/might/could = uncertain possibility.

title: PRESENT DEDUCTION
notes:
✓ For conclusions about what is true now, use modal + base verb or modal + be.

✓ He must be tired.
✓ She may be at home.
✓ They might be busy.
✓ He could be sick.
✓ She can't be serious.

✓ With a normal verb → modal + V1.
✓ He must know the answer.
✓ She may live nearby.

✓ With an adjective/noun/place → modal + be.
✓ He must be tired.
✓ She may be a teacher.
✓ They could be at school.

✓ Structure → modal + V1 / be + complement.

title: DEDUCTION ABOUT PAST EVENTS
notes:
✓ To make deductions about the past, use modal + have + V3.

✓ MUST HAVE + V3 → strong conclusion about a past event.
✓ She must have forgotten the meeting.

✓ MAY/MIGHT/COULD HAVE + V3 → possible past event.
✓ He may have missed the bus.
✓ She might have gone home.
✓ They could have taken the wrong road.

✓ CAN'T/COULDN'T HAVE + V3 → strong conclusion that a past event was impossible.
✓ He can't have forgotten; I reminded him twice.

✓ Formula → modal + have + past participle (V3).

title: MUST HAVE + V3
notes:
✓ Must have + V3 → strong logical conclusion about something that happened in the past.

✓ The streets are wet. It must have rained.
✓ She looks exhausted. She must have worked all night.
✓ They arrived late. They must have missed the earlier train.

✓ Meaning → the speaker did not directly observe the event but concludes that it happened from evidence.

⚠ Must have + V3 is NOT the same as had to + V1.

✓ She must have left early. → deduction.
✓ She had to leave early. → necessity/obligation.

title: MAY/MIGHT/COULD HAVE + V3
notes:
✓ May have + V3 → possible past event.
✓ He may have forgotten.

✓ Might have + V3 → possible past event, often more tentative.
✓ She might have taken the wrong bus.

✓ Could have + V3 → possible explanation or possible past event.
✓ They could have missed the train.

✓ These structures show uncertainty about what actually happened.

⚠ Could have can also express an unrealized possibility/ability.
✓ I could have won the race. → it was possible, but I did not.

✓ Context determines the meaning.

title: CAN'T HAVE / COULDN'T HAVE + V3
notes:
✓ Can't have + V3 → strong deduction that something did not happen.
✓ She can't have forgotten the meeting; I called her this morning.

✓ Couldn't have + V3 → strong belief that something was impossible in the past.
✓ He couldn't have stolen the money; he was abroad.

✓ Meaning → evidence makes the past event impossible or extremely unlikely.

⚠ This is different from simple inability.

✓ He couldn't swim. → lack of ability.
✓ He couldn't have swum across the river. → past event judged impossible.

title: FUTURE POSSIBILITY
notes:
✓ Future possibility can be expressed with may, might, could, and other structures.

✓ It may rain tomorrow.
✓ It might rain tomorrow.
✓ It could rain tomorrow.

✓ Will → stronger prediction, not normally just a weak possibility.
✓ It will probably rain tomorrow.

✓ Should/ought to → expected or probable result.
✓ The package should arrive tomorrow.

✓ Rough scale →
may/might/could = possible
should/ought to = probable/expected
will = confident prediction.

title: DEGREES OF CERTAINTY
notes:
✓ MUST → very strong positive deduction.

✓ SHOULD / OUGHT TO → expectation or strong probability.

✓ MAY → possible.

✓ MIGHT → possible, often more tentative.

✓ COULD → possible explanation/alternative.

✓ CAN'T / CANNOT → very strong negative deduction.

✓ COULDN'T → impossible or extremely unlikely in a particular context, especially past situations.

⚠ There is no exact universal percentage for each modal. Context, intonation, and speaker intention affect the strength of certainty.

title: SHOULD FOR PROBABILITY
notes:
✓ Should + V1 can express expectation or probability rather than obligation.

✓ The bus should arrive soon.
→ I expect it to arrive soon.

✓ She should be home by now.
→ I expect that she is home now.

✓ They should have arrived already.
→ I expect they have arrived.

✓ Should is weaker than must when making a logical deduction.

✓ He must be home. → very strong conclusion.
✓ He should be home. → expected, but less certain.

title: MODAL + BE + V-ING
notes:
✓ Modal + be + V-ing → possibility or deduction about an action happening around a particular time.

✓ She must be sleeping.
→ strong deduction that she is sleeping now.

✓ He may be working.
→ possible that he is working now.

✓ They might be waiting for us.
→ possible ongoing action.

✓ He can't be driving; his car is here.

✓ Formula → modal + be + V-ing.

✓ This structure emphasizes an action in progress.

title: MODAL + HAVE BEEN + V-ING
notes:
✓ Modal + have been + V-ing → deduction or possibility about an ongoing activity in the past.

✓ She must have been studying all night.
✓ He may have been sleeping when you called.
✓ They might have been waiting for hours.
✓ He can't have been working all day; I saw him playing football.

✓ Formula → modal + have been + V-ing.

✓ Use this when the duration or ongoing nature of the past activity is important.

title: DEDUCTION WITH DIFFERENT VERB FORMS
notes:
✓ Present state → modal + V1 / be.
✓ He must be tired.

✓ Present action in progress → modal + be + V-ing.
✓ He must be sleeping.

✓ Past completed event → modal + have + V3.
✓ He must have slept badly.

✓ Past action in progress → modal + have been + V-ing.
✓ He must have been sleeping when I called.

✓ Time + aspect both matter when choosing the structure.

title: POSSIBILITY IN QUESTIONS
notes:
✓ Modal verbs can be used in questions to ask about possible situations.

✓ Could he be at home?
✓ Might she know the answer?
✓ Could they have missed the train?
✓ Might he have forgotten?

✓ May is possible in formal questions but is less common for ordinary possibility questions.

✓ May he be at home? → formal/less common.

✓ Could is particularly common when asking about possible explanations.

title: DEDUCTION FROM EVIDENCE
notes:
✓ Deduction usually depends on evidence.

✓ The lights are on and the car is outside. → They must be home.

✓ The office is locked and everyone has gone. → They can't be inside.

✓ Her phone is switched off. → She might be sleeping.

✓ The ground is wet. → It must have rained.

✓ Evidence → logical conclusion.

✓ Strong evidence → must/can't.
✓ Limited evidence → may/might/could.
✓ Expected evidence/result → should/ought to.

title: MUST NOT VS CAN'T
notes:
✓ Mustn't / must not → prohibition or strong instruction.
✓ You mustn't touch this machine.

✓ Can't → negative deduction.
✓ He can't be at home; I just saw him outside.

✓ Compare →
You mustn't enter. → You are prohibited from entering.
He can't be inside. → I conclude that he is not inside.

⚠ For logical negative deduction, use can't/cannot rather than mustn't.

title: POSSIBILITY VS DEDUCTION
notes:
✓ POSSIBILITY → the speaker considers something possible but does not have enough evidence for a strong conclusion.
✓ She might be at home.

✓ DEDUCTION → the speaker uses evidence to reach a conclusion.
✓ The lights are on, so she must be at home.

✓ NEGATIVE DEDUCTION → evidence strongly suggests something is impossible/untrue.
✓ The office is locked, so she can't be inside.

✓ Key distinction → possibility = one possible explanation; deduction = conclusion based on evidence.

title: COULD HAVE: TWO IMPORTANT MEANINGS
notes:
✓ Meaning 1 → possible past explanation.
✓ He could have missed the bus.
→ It is possible that he missed it.

✓ Meaning 2 → unrealized past possibility/ability.
✓ He could have won the race, but he fell.
→ Winning was possible, but it did not happen.

✓ Context determines the meaning.

✓ She could have taken the wrong road. → possible explanation.
✓ She could have taken the earlier train, but she chose not to. → available but unrealized option.

title: MIGHT HAVE: POSSIBILITY VS REGRET
notes:
✓ Might have + V3 can express past possibility.
✓ He might have forgotten.

✓ It can also occur in contexts suggesting an unrealized possibility or criticism.
✓ You might have told me! → criticism that you did not tell me.

✓ Meaning depends strongly on context and intonation.

⚠ In deduction questions, focus on the possibility meaning when evidence is uncertain.

title: COMMON EXAM PATTERNS
notes:
✓ The lights are on. They _____ be at home.
✓ Answer → must

✓ She isn't answering. She _____ be sleeping.
✓ Answer → may/might/could

✓ He is in London today. He _____ be in Addis Ababa now.
✓ Answer → can't

✓ The streets are wet. It _____ have rained.
✓ Answer → must

✓ She didn't arrive. She _____ have missed the bus.
✓ Answer → may/might/could

✓ He was with me all evening. He _____ have committed the crime at that time.
✓ Answer → can't/couldn't

✓ The train should arrive soon. → expected probability.

✓ Exam clue → look for evidence words such as 'because', 'I saw', 'the lights are on', 'he was there', 'the ground is wet', and 'I know that...' to identify deduction.

title: COMMON ERRORS
notes:
❌ He must to be tired.
✓ He must be tired.

❌ She may to come.
✓ She may come.

❌ He might comes later.
✓ He might come later.

❌ They must have went home.
✓ They must have gone home.

❌ She may has forgotten.
✓ She may have forgotten.

❌ He must has been working.
✓ He must have been working.

❌ He mustn't be at home. → if you mean deduction.
✓ He can't be at home.

❌ It can rain tomorrow. → for ordinary specific possibility.
✓ It may/might/could rain tomorrow.

❌ She must have to be tired. → incorrect for deduction.
✓ She must be tired.

✓ Modal rule → modal + base verb.
✓ Perfect modal → modal + have + V3.

title: MASTER FORMULA TABLE
notes:
✓ PRESENT POSSIBILITY → may/might/could + V1/be.
✓ She may be home.

✓ PRESENT DEDUCTION → must + V1/be.
✓ She must be home.

✓ PRESENT NEGATIVE DEDUCTION → can't + V1/be.
✓ She can't be home.

✓ PAST POSSIBILITY → may/might/could + have + V3.
✓ She might have gone home.

✓ PAST DEDUCTION → must + have + V3.
✓ She must have gone home.

✓ PAST NEGATIVE DEDUCTION → can't/couldn't + have + V3.
✓ She can't have gone home.

✓ PRESENT CONTINUOUS DEDUCTION → must/may/might/could + be + V-ing.
✓ She must be sleeping.

✓ PAST CONTINUOUS DEDUCTION → must/may/might/could + have been + V-ing.
✓ She must have been sleeping.

title: POSSIBILITY & DEDUCTION: EXAM GUIDE
notes:
◆ 1. Identify the time → present, past, or future.

◆ 2. Decide whether the meaning is possibility or deduction.

◆ 3. Estimate certainty → strong, medium, weak, or impossible.

◆ 4. Choose the modal → must, should, may, might, could, can't, couldn't.

◆ 5. Check whether the action is ongoing.

◆ 6. If it refers to a completed past event → use modal + have + V3.

◆ 7. If it refers to a continuing past action → use modal + have been + V-ing.

◆ 8. Check the evidence provided in the sentence.

✓ QUICK MEMORY:
✓ MUST → strong positive deduction.
✓ SHOULD/OUGHT TO → expected/probable.
✓ MAY → possible.
✓ MIGHT → possible/tentative.
✓ COULD → possible explanation.
✓ CAN'T → strong negative deduction.
✓ COULDN'T → past impossibility.

✓ Golden rule → Modal verbs are followed by the base form of the verb. For past deduction or possibility, use HAVE + V3.

✓ Present → must be / may be / might be / could be / can't be.
✓ Past → must have been / may have been / might have been / could have been / can't have been.
✓ Ongoing → modal + be + V-ing.
✓ Past ongoing → modal + have been + V-ing.
